title: Finding a Deceased Loved One's Money in Florida (November 2026)
summary: Elayne's Nov 2026 guide covers finding a deceased loved one's Florida unclaimed property, who can claim it, and what documents are needed.
body_markdown:
Florida holds money and other financial assets that were turned over to the state as unclaimed property, including assets that belonged to a person who has died. Whether a claim can be made depends on the claimant’s legal entitlement to the property, and a new[probate](https://www.elayne.com/resources/probate-explained-what-happens-after-someone-dies-and-how-to-plan-ahead) case is not always required. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: how to search FLTreasureHunt.gov, who has the legal authority to claim, how the small estate affidavit works, what documents are required, how the 90-day review period works, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- FLTreasureHunt.gov is Florida’s official site for free searches by a deceased loved one’s name.
- Claims require proof of legal entitlement, plus identification and proof of death.
- Florida’s 90-day review period starts when the state receives a complete claim package.


## What Is Florida Unclaimed Property?


Florida unclaimed property is money or other financial assets turned over to the state after remaining inactive or uncollected. Businesses report these assets when they cannot reconnect with the owner and return the property.


As a historical example, Florida’s Division of Unclaimed Property reported returning over $44 million in March 2025. For families settling an estate, a Florida unclaimed property search may reveal funds belonging to a loved one who died.

## Types of Property That End Up Unclaimed


- Bank accounts left inactive.
- Uncashed checks, including payroll checks.
- Life insurance proceeds that were never collected.
- Stocks and unpaid dividends.
- Utility deposits and refunds.
- Contents from abandoned safe deposit boxes.


Old statements or insurance paperwork can provide clues when[finding assets of a deceased person](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-assets-deceased-person) , even when the family no longer has access to the original account.


## How Florida's Dormancy Periods Work


Under Chapter 717, Florida Statutes, a dormancy period is how long property remains unclaimed before reporting is required.[Florida’s property-specific dormancy periods](https://unclaimed.org/reporting/florida/) include:


Property type Period


Checking and savings accounts 5 years


Certificates of deposit 5 years


Matured life insurance 2 years


Safe deposit boxes 3 years


Securities 3 years


Traveler’s checks 15 years


## How to Search Florida Unclaimed Property for a Deceased Person


On FLTreasureHunt.gov, an unclaimed property search uses a deceased loved one’s name in the free, daily-updated property database.


1. The Florida property search page starts with “Person” and the loved one’s name.
2. Results show a “CLAIM” button beside each property record.
3. Selected records enter “CLAIMED PROPERTY CART,” where the claim-form process begins.


For ties to other states, MissingMoney’s free name search expands the[unclaimed inheritance search](https://www.elayne.com/resources/unclaimed-property-and-inheritance-search-guide) .


## Who Has the Legal Authority to Claim a Deceased Person's Property


Claiming a deceased person’s Florida unclaimed property requires proof of legal entitlement. Finding the listing does not grant authority.


- A surviving spouse or named beneficiary may claim with proof of entitlement.
- An executor or administrator may act under letters testamentary or letters of administration.
- An estate affidavit may allow beneficiaries to claim without a probate court order. Under[Florida’s small estate account requirements](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&Search_String=&URL=0700-0799/0717/Sections/0717.1243.html) :


- All abandoned property held by the department for the owner must total $20,000 or less.
- No probate proceeding may be pending.
- All beneficiaries must sign the affidavit and agree on division of the estate.
- The affidavit must state that funeral expenses, expenses of the last illness, and other lawful claims have been paid.
- The claim must include a copy of any will and any additional information reasonably necessary to prove entitlement.


## What Documentation Is Required to File a Claim


Each Florida unclaimed property claim form lists its required documents. For a deceased owner, the package typically includes:


- A completed, signed claim form.
- Current government-issued identification for the claimant.
- Proof of death, usually a death certificate.
- Documents supporting entitlement, such as a will or court-issued letters testamentary or letters of administration, depending on the claim.


Requirements vary by claim type. Under[Florida’s claim-review statute](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&Search_String=&URL=0700-0799/0717/Sections/0717.124.html) , the state generally decides a claim within 90 days of receiving it. When the state asks for more information, the 90 days run from the date the response is received. Statutory extensions may apply.


For example, a court-appointed personal representative might submit identification and a death certificate but omit the letters of administration showing authority to act for the estate. If the state requests those letters, the review period runs from receipt of the response instead of the original claim. The missing proof of authority can delay the decision.

## How Elayne Helps Families Find What a Loved One Left Behind


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) is an online service that helps families settle an estate after a death.


Asset Search is the step that looks for accounts, benefits, and debts, including property turned over to a state as unclaimed property.


For context, no single record lists everything a person had. A will names who receives what, but it does not list accounts. Details about accounts are spread across mail, statements, tax records, and databases such as FLTreasureHunt.gov.


Elayne holds IRS authorization to request IRS tax transcripts for the person who passed. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. It is a record of what banks, employers, and insurers reported about the person to the IRS, covering 10 years. Each entry names an institution that had a financial relationship with the person.


Elayne also requests the person’s Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, debts, cards, and credit lines in the person’s name. More than 100 other sources are checked, including:


- Life insurance locators: the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) Policy Locator, which covers in-force and lapsed policies, and MIB, which covers insurance application activity across about 400 carriers.
- Pension registry: the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) registry of unclaimed pensions from terminated plans.
- Unclaimed property: MissingMoney.com, the national unclaimed property database, plus state unclaimed property searches.
- Property and vehicle records: deeds, mortgages, liens, and vehicles titled in the person’s name.
- Crypto exchange accounts, searched when the tax transcripts or the estate record point to crypto.
- Veterans benefits: VA life insurance and unclaimed veterans insurance funds, searched when the estate record shows veteran status.


Every finding is listed with the institution and record it came from, which forms a source-attributed estate inventory. Debts appear alongside assets, so what the estate owes is visible before anything is paid out. The IRS transcripts also show whether the estate owes the IRS anything.


Legal authority decides how much of the search can run. That authority comes from the court, not from Elayne and not from being named in a will. In court terms, it is documented as letters of administration or letters testamentary, depending on the state and whether a will exists. Portions of the search can run before the court issues it, and the full search opens once it is in place. Elayne is an eligible estate expense, paid from the estate or reimbursed by it.


## FAQ


### Where can families look for a loved one’s life insurance if FLTreasureHunt.gov shows no results?


The NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator offers a free search for policies that may still be held by insurers and would not appear in a Florida unclaimed property search. NAIC, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, forwards requests to participating insurers; an insurer contacts the requester if it finds a match and the requester is entitled to information about the policy.


### What if money is found on FLTreasureHunt.gov after a loved one’s estate is already closed?


A closed estate does not prevent a claim, but the state still needs proof of the claimant’s entitlement to the money. Existing probate orders may support the claim; if they do not cover the newly found property, an estate attorney can advise whether further court proceedings are needed.


### How can families confirm that a FLTreasureHunt.gov listing belongs to a loved one when the name is common?


A matching name alone is not enough; details about the reporting business and the owner’s past location can help distinguish a loved one’s property from another person’s. Old bank statements, insurance records, and utility bills can support the connection, and the Division of Unclaimed Property can explain what proof the claim requires.


### Does the state charge a fee to search for or claim a deceased person’s unclaimed property?


No. Searching the state database is free, and the Division states that owners and heirs have the right to claim property at no cost. Fees can apply if a claimant chooses to hire a private recovery firm under a signed agreement.


### Which name variations does a Florida unclaimed property search cover?


The Division’s guidance is to search every name that may be tied to the property: current and previous names, maiden names, married names, business names, and common spelling variations. A deceased person’s property can be listed under any of these, depending on how the reporting business recorded the name.


### Why might recently reported property not appear in the database yet?


Holders such as banks, insurers, and utilities file their reports with the Division each year, before May 1, covering the previous calendar year. Division staff review, reconcile, and process those reports before the property becomes searchable. Newly reported property may not appear right away, and it becomes available for claims once processing is complete.
